text:
The three days of travel in Genesis 22 have the character of a suspended sentence. During them nothing outward happens; yet everything of significance happens. The servants are named, and the wood, the knife, and the fire; thus the instruments of the act are given before the act itself occurs. The story keeps obedience and horror together, and allows neither obedience nor horror to prevail. Faith, in this story, has the form of a structured relation or arrangement; it is no mere report of feeling.

When this scene is compared with the earlier promise, the apparent difference between them is narrowed. Isaac is the child of the covenant, the one through whom the nations are to be blessed; and the chapter turns that promise into a test. The scene depends on the single word hineni, "here I am," spoken by Abraham three times, once to God, once to Isaac, and once to the angel. In each use the word has another meaning; in each successive use it costs him more. The language of presence is here also the language of loss.
